morphology.size: ~6-15 x 0.1-0.2 µm — below the resolution of light microscopy without special methods
morphology.motility: Motile with a corkscrew rotational and flexing motion via periplasmic flagella
morphology.notes: Does not Gram stain well due to its thinness; visualized by dark-field microscopy or direct fluorescent antibody testing

habitat.naturalHabitat: Exclusively human host — no environmental or animal reservoir
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Does not survive outside the host

microscopy.appearance: Thin, tightly coiled spirochetes, too thin to be seen by standard bright-field/Gram stain

culture.media: Cannot be cultured on artificial media in vitro
culture.growthCharacteristics: Obligate parasite — historically propagated only in rabbit testes for research

identificationClues: Cannot be cultured on standard laboratory media
Diagnosis relies on serology (nontreponemal: VDRL/RPR; treponemal: FTA-ABS, TPPA) or dark-field microscopy of lesion exudate
Thin spiral organism, invisible on Gram stain
Progresses through primary (chancre), secondary, latent, and tertiary stages

virulenceFactors: Outer membrane proteins facilitating adhesion and immune evasion
Ability to disseminate widely and establish latency
clinicalImportance.transmission: Sexual contact; transplacental (congenital syphilis); rarely blood transfusion
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: Sexually transmitted infection with rising incidence in many regions; untreated infection can progress over years to tertiary syphilis affecting the cardiovascular and central nervous systems
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: Diagnosis is serologic, not culture-based, since the organism cannot be grown in vitro

examFacts.importantTest: VDRL/RPR (nontreponemal) confirmed by FTA-ABS or TPPA (treponemal); dark-field microscopy of chancre fluid
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: Cannot be grown on artificial media — one of very few major bacterial pathogens still diagnosed purely by serology/microscopy
